The long facade of the National Palace defines the eastern side of the Zócalo. The building is closely linked to Mexico's political history and remains an active government site. Even from the square, visitors can appreciate its length and its place in the architectural ensemble of the historic centre.

Inside, the palace is known for its historic murals and courtyards. Access to the interior depends on current arrangements: official events may restrict visits. You can plan a walk across the Zócalo with confidence, but entry to the palace should be confirmed separately for your particular trip.

Necochea lies on the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires Province. For travellers, it is a seaside destination; for an agricultural delegation, it offers a chance to explore the connection between the agricultural Pampas and export logistics.

We include Necochea on the route between Tres Arroyos and Mar del Plata. You can stop here for lunch before continuing along the Atlantic coast. An interest in grain exports does not automatically grant access to port facilities: if your group needs a separate technical visit, we will agree on its scope and feasibility in advance.

Neko Harbour lies on the mainland coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, in Andvord Bay. A small beach and rocky stretches of shoreline are surrounded by towering mountain peaks and heavily crevassed glaciers. Ice cliffs and floating ice create one of the characteristic landscapes of the peninsula's western side.

Gentoo penguins nest along the shore; skuas and kelp gulls can be seen in the surrounding area, while Weddell seals regularly come ashore to rest. The glaciers around Neko Harbour actively calve ice, so the expedition team chooses where to observe and whether a landing is possible according to conditions. A visit to the harbour on an itinerary should be understood as a possible stop, not a guaranteed landing.

Neptune's Bellows connects the sea with Port Foster, the bay within Deception Island. Ships pass through this narrow channel to enter the flooded caldera of an active volcano. Dark rocky shores with patches of snow form a natural gateway, opening onto a broad inner bay.

You can watch the passage through Neptune's Bellows from the deck of an expedition ship. Just beyond the entrance, to the northeast, lies Whalers Bay, with historic remains of the whaling industry. Entering the caldera and making any subsequent landings depend on the captain's decision, the weather and the island's current visitor regulations.
